193.title: You are the Christ (Mark 8:27–30)
193.hook: at Caesarea Philippi, Peter says it: you are the Messiah, the anointed one
193.carry: who do you say I am?
193.howItsDone: Christians of every church confess Jesus as the Christ, and many say it aloud in the Creeds on Sundays; some Christians use Peter's question as a regular prompt for personal prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a blind man at Bethsaida saw men like trees, walking, and only then saw clearly. Your line was sight comes in stages. Did something come a little clearer? Day one hundred ninety-three.

Think of the way people talk about someone new at work before anyone really knows them. He's the one who used to be at that other place. She's like the last manager, only quieter. Everybody has a theory. Now Mark takes us far north, to the villages around a town called Caesarea Philippi, near the springs where the Jordan River begins. Jesus and his friends are walking, and on the road he asks a simple question: "Whom do men say that I am?" They have the gossip ready. Some say John the Baptist, back from the dead. Some say Elijah. Some say one of the prophets. Then he turns the question around, and there's nowhere to hide: "But whom say ye that I am?" And Peter answers.
screen: `A ROAD FAR IN THE NORTH.` → `WHOM DO MEN SAY THAT I AM?` → `BUT WHOM SAY YE?`

segments.voice: Peter says four words in the old King James Bible: "Thou art the Christ." And here's the thing most people never hear. Christ is not Jesus's last name. There was no Mr. and Mrs. Christ. It's a title. The Greek word is Christos, and it means the anointed one. It translates a Hebrew word, mashiach, which comes into English as Messiah. Anointed means oil poured on your head. In the Hebrew Bible, the prophet Samuel pours oil on young David to mark him as king, and priests were anointed too. So by Jesus's day, many Jews hoped for an anointed one, a king from David's family, who would set things right. When Peter says Christ, he's saying: you are that one. Notice where this sits. It's almost exactly the middle of Mark. For eight chapters people have been asking who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him. Now someone finally says it out loud. Mark's very first line had already told the reader: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." The disciples just took half the book to catch up. And then the strangest part: Jesus tells them to tell no one. Scholars have argued for over a century about why Mark keeps this secret, and Mark never fully explains. One strong hint comes in the very next scene: the word Christ meant something different to Peter than it would turn out to mean. For Christians of every church, this is the heart of the faith: Jesus is the Christ. But notice how he asked. Not what do people say. What do you say.
screen: `WHOM SAY YE THAT I AM?` · `CHRIST IS A TITLE, NOT A SURNAME.` · `ANOINTED: OIL ON A KING'S HEAD.` · `THE HINGE OF MARK: TELL NO ONE.` · then, large: `THOU ART THE CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the question be asked of you. Settle, and breathe slowly. Maybe you pray to Jesus every day. Maybe you're learning about him for someone you love. Maybe you honestly don't know. Imagine the road, the walking, and the question turned toward you: who do you say I am? Don't reach for the right answer, or the answer your family gives. Find your own word, even if it's teacher, or stranger, or I'm not sure yet. If you pray, you can simply say what you find. Just be honest. The bell holds the time.
Christ. From the Greek Christos, the anointed one, the same word as the Hebrew Messiah. A title, not a surname.
Your line: who do you say I am? Today, notice one time you repeat what others say about someone, and ask what you'd say yourself. Day one hundred ninety-three.

194.title: Take up your cross (Mark 8:31–38)
194.hook: Peter rebukes him about suffering, is called Satan, and hears: lose your life to save it
194.howItsDone: Many Christians speak of their own small sacrifices as carrying the cross, and some take on a daily act of self-giving; in Lent especially, many churches invite people to give something up for the sake of others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, on the road near Caesarea Philippi, Peter called him the Christ, the anointed one. Your line was who do you say I am? What did you find when you asked it? Day one hundred ninety-four.

You know the feeling of getting the answer right in front of everyone. Peter has just had that moment. Thou art the Christ. Top of the class. And then, straight away, Jesus starts to explain what that will mean, and it's the last thing anyone wants to hear. He'll suffer many things. He'll be rejected by the elders and the chief priests and the scribes. He'll be killed. And after three days he'll rise again. Mark adds that he said it openly, no riddles this time. So Peter does what any loyal friend might do. He takes Jesus aside, quietly, and tells him off. No. Not that. Not you. And Jesus turns around, looks at the others, and answers Peter in front of all of them.
screen: `TOP OF THE CLASS.` → `HE MUST SUFFER.` → `PETER TAKES HIM ASIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the answer, in the old King James Bible: "Get thee behind me, Satan." From top of the class to Satan in five verses. It sounds brutal, but listen to the word. In Hebrew, satan means an adversary, the one who stands in your way. Peter has put himself on the road, in front of Jesus, blocking it. Get behind me: go back to following. Then Jesus calls the whole crowd over and says the line people have repeated ever since: "Whosoever will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me." To us a cross is a necklace or a steeple. To them it was nothing of the kind. It was how Rome executed rebels and slaves, in public, and the condemned often carried the crossbeam themselves. The crowd would have flinched. And then the riddle at the center: "For whosoever will save his life shall lose it; but whosoever shall lose his life for my sake and the gospel's, the same shall save it." Grip your life too tightly and it slips away. Spend it on something bigger and you find it. Christians have read this in more than one way. For the early church, under persecution, it could mean dying for the faith. Luke's version adds the word daily, and many hear it as ordinary, everyday self-giving: the parent up at 3am, the friend who shows up. And many churches today say plainly what it does not mean: it is not a command to stay in harm or abuse. What they share is the shape: love costs something, and the cost is where life is found.
screen: `FROM TOP OF THE CLASS TO SATAN.` · `SATAN: THE ONE IN THE WAY.` · `A CROSS WAS AN EXECUTION.` · `LOSE IT TO FIND IT.` · then, large: `TAKE UP HIS CROSS, AND FOLLOW ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one small thing to give up for someone today. Settle, and breathe. Think of one person. What would make their day lighter? Maybe it's your turn to choose the show, or the last slice, or twenty minutes you'd planned for yourself. Something that costs a little, not a lot. Picture yourself handing it over. Notice what your hands want to do: hold on. If you pray, you can offer it to God as part of following. If you don't, just decide. The bell holds the time.
Take up your cross. In Jesus's day, the walk of the condemned. In Christian life, following him when it costs something.
Your line: lose it to find it. Today, give the thing away, and watch whether you feel smaller or larger afterward. Day one hundred ninety-four.

195.title: Listen to him (Mark 9:1–13)
195.hook: the transfiguration, and the one instruction from the cloud: listen to him
195.howItsDone: Many churches celebrate the Transfiguration as a feast, on August 6 in the Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican calendars, and many Protestant churches read the story on the Sunday before Lent; Christians often speak of listening to Jesus through reading the Gospels and in silent prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter stood in the road and heard take up your cross. Your line was lose it to find it. What did you give away, and how did it feel? Day one hundred ninety-five.

Six days later, Mark says, Jesus takes three friends, Peter, James and John, up a high mountain, just the four of them. And up there, he changes in front of them. His clothes turn shining, dazzling white, and Mark, who loves a homely detail, says they were whiter than any laundryman on earth could get them. Then two figures appear beside him, talking with him: Elijah and Moses, great prophets from centuries before. And Peter, bless him, has to say something. It's good for us to be here! Let's build three shelters: one for you, one for Moses, one for Elijah. And Mark adds, gently: "For he wist not what to say; for they were sore afraid." He didn't know what to say, so he said something. We have all been Peter.
screen: `A HIGH MOUNTAIN, JUST FOUR.` → `WHITER THAN ANY LAUNDRY.` → `LET'S BUILD THREE SHELTERS.`

segments.voice: While Peter is still planning construction, a cloud comes down and covers them, and a voice speaks out of it. In the King James Bible: "This is my beloved Son: hear him." That's it. One sentence of introduction, one instruction. Not build. Not explain. Hear him. The Greek word means listen, and in the Bible listening is never just sound in the ears. In Hebrew, the same word covers hearing and obeying. To really listen is to let it change what you do. Notice what the voice doesn't say. It doesn't say listen to Moses and Elijah too. Many Christians read those two as standing for the Law and the Prophets, the whole Hebrew Bible, gathered around Jesus. And then, suddenly, they look around and see no one any more, only Jesus, with them. The cloud is gone. The glow is gone. What's left is an ordinary man on a mountain, and the instruction to listen to him. Mark never names the mountain. Christian tradition since early centuries has pointed to Mount Tabor in Galilee, and others suggest Mount Hermon, much nearer Caesarea Philippi. The text is silent. On the way down he tells them to tell no one until he has risen from the dead, and they puzzle over what rising from the dead could mean. Christians call this the transfiguration, from the Latin for being changed in form. Orthodox Christians hold it especially dear, and Catholic, Anglican and many other churches keep it as a feast on the sixth of August.
screen: `A CLOUD, AND ONE SENTENCE.` · `LISTEN MEANS HEAR AND DO.` · `NO ONE LEFT BUT JESUS.` · `A MOUNTAIN MARK NEVER NAMES.` · then, large: `THIS IS MY BELOVED SON: HEAR HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be the one who listens. Settle, and breathe. For the next two minutes, don't plan anything, don't fix anything, don't build any shelters. Just listen. First the sounds of the room. Then the sounds beyond it, far away. Then the quiet underneath. If you pray, you can hold the line hear him, and wait, without filling the silence. If a thought wants to talk, let it pass like a cloud. The bell holds the time.
Listen to him. The one instruction from the cloud. In the Bible, listening means hearing and letting it change what you do.
Your line: listen to him. Today, in one conversation, listen more than you speak. When you feel the urge to build three shelters, wait. Day one hundred ninety-five.

196.title: Help my unbelief (Mark 9:14–29)
196.hook: a desperate father: I believe; help my unbelief
196.howItsDone: Many Christians pray the father's words, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief," as a short prayer in times of doubt, and pastors often point to this story to say that faith and doubt can live together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, on the mountain, a voice from the cloud gave one instruction. Your line was listen to him. Did you manage to listen more than you spoke? Day one hundred ninety-six. The end of another week.

From the shining mountain straight down into a mess. At the bottom there's a crowd, and an argument. The disciples who stayed behind have tried to heal a boy, and they couldn't. The boy's father pushes through. His son, he says, has a spirit that takes his speech, throws him to the ground, makes him foam and grind his teeth and go rigid. Since he was a child. It has thrown him into fire and into water. Any parent who has sat up all night in a hospital knows this man. He's tried everything, and now even the disciples have failed. So when he gets to Jesus, his hope is worn thin. In the King James Bible he says: "if thou canst do any thing, have compassion on us, and help us." If.
screen: `DOWN FROM THE MOUNTAIN.` → `THE DISCIPLES COULDN'T.` → `IF THOU CANST DO ANY THING.`

segments.voice: Jesus catches the word. If you can? "All things are possible to him that believeth." And the father cries out, with tears, the most honest prayer in the Gospels: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Both at once. I believe, and I don't. I trust you, and I'm terrified. He doesn't pretend. And here's what matters: Jesus doesn't send him away to come back when his faith is tidier. He heals the boy, and lifts him by the hand. Half a faith, handed over honestly, is enough to start with. The Greek word for unbelief is apistia, faith with a no in front of it. Many Christians find this verse a lifeline, because it says doubt and faith can live in the same heart, in the same sentence. Readers today often notice that the boy's signs sound like epilepsy. Mark describes a spirit, and Christians understand stories like this in different ways; the text simply tells it as Mark heard it. Later, the disciples ask why they failed. His answer: this kind comes out only by prayer. The King James adds and fasting, but the oldest Greek manuscripts don't have those words. Now look back at the week. Seven baskets: enough again. Hard hearts in a boat: do you not yet understand? A blind man seeing men like trees. Peter: you are the Christ. Take up your cross. Listen to him. And now this father. Every one of them sees partly, and is helped the rest of the way.
screen: `IF THOU CANST?` · `I BELIEVE; HELP MY UNBELIEF.` · `ONLY BY PRAYER.` · `A WEEK OF SEEING IN PART.` · then, large: `LORD, I BELIEVE; HELP THOU MINE UNBELIEF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold both halves honestly. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you trust, and one thing you doubt. About God, about yourself, about someone you love. Don't solve either one. Just let them sit side by side. If you pray, you can say the father's words, slowly, as many times as you like: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. If you don't pray, you can simply say: some of me trusts, some of me doesn't, and that's where I am. The bell holds the time.
Help my unbelief. A father's prayer with belief and doubt in one breath, and it was enough.
Your line: help my unbelief. Today, when you feel only half sure, don't wait to be certain. Bring the half you have. Day one hundred ninety-six.
